lead: Solving a nonlinear state equation is usually impossible, so stability must be judged without solving it. A Lyapunov function V(x) is an energy-like scalar, positive everywhere except at the equilibrium, that never increases along a trajectory. If V always falls, the equilibrium is asymptotically stable. The test needs one scalar function and one derivative, not a closed-form solution. Engineers use it to certify aircraft, power converters, robot arms and motor drives.
prereq: You need: the state model and state transition matrix of Unit 6, State Space Analysis, and the stability definitions of Unit 3, Stability and Root Locus.

sections.h3: Equilibrium points and what stability means

blocks.text: A nonlinear autonomous system is written ẋ = f(x). Here x is the n×1 state vector, ẋ is its time derivative, and f is a nonlinear vector function. An equilibrium point x_e is a state where the system stops moving: f(x_e) = 0. A pendulum hanging straight down, a motor at rest, a DC-DC converter at its set point — each has such a state.
Shift the coordinates so the equilibrium sits at the origin: replace x by x − x_e. Every definition below is then about the origin, and x = 0 means the system is exactly at equilibrium.

The equilibrium is stable (in the Lyapunov sense) if for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that ||x(0)|| < δ guarantees ||x(t)|| < ε for all t ≥ 0. Here ||x|| = √(x₁² + … + xₙ²) is the distance from the origin. Start close enough and you stay close forever, though you may never arrive.

The equilibrium is asymptotically stable if it is stable and x(t) → 0 as t → ∞. The set of starting points that end at the origin is the region of attraction. If that region is the whole state space, the origin is globally asymptotically stable.
Linearising answers a local question only, and when the Jacobian eigenvalues sit on the imaginary axis it answers nothing. A Lyapunov function can settle the whole state space in one calculation.

sections.h3: The Lyapunov function and the direct method

blocks.text: A Lyapunov function is a scalar function V(x), continuous with continuous partial derivatives, that behaves like stored energy. Two conditions make it admissible: V(0) = 0, and V(x) > 0 for every x ≠ 0. This is called positive definite. A bowl shape is the picture to keep.
Differentiate V along the trajectories of the system, using the chain rule:

blocks.where: V̇ (read V-dot) is the rate of change of V along a solution; ∇V is the row vector of partial derivatives; ẋᵢ is replaced by the i-th component of f(x). No solution x(t) is needed.

items: V̇(x) ≤ 0 everywhere → the origin is stable.
V̇(x) < 0 for every x ≠ 0 (negative definite) → the origin is asymptotically stable.
V̇ < 0 and V(x) → ∞ as ||x|| → ∞ → the origin is globally asymptotically stable.

blocks.text: The last extra condition is radial unboundedness: V must grow without limit in every direction, so the level curves cannot flatten out and leave a distant region where V̇ is silent. Some syllabi call this approach the direct method or Lyapunov's second method.

items: Write the system as ẋ = f(x) with the equilibrium moved to the origin.
Propose V(x): a quadratic form ½xᵀx, a sum of squares, or the physical energy of the plant.
Check V(0) = 0 and V(x) > 0 for x ≠ 0.
Compute V̇ = ∇V · f(x) and simplify, cancelling cross terms.
Test the sign of V̇; check radial unboundedness before claiming a global result.

blocks.text: The method proves stability without solving anything, but it is only sufficient. Failing to find a V proves nothing, and no general recipe exists for inventing one.

sections.h3: Linear systems and the Lyapunov equation

blocks.text: For the linear system ẋ = Ax, try V(x) = xᵀPx, where P is a symmetric positive definite matrix. Positive definiteness of P is exactly the condition V(x) > 0 for x ≠ 0. Differentiating gives:

blocks.where: A is the n×n system matrix; P and Q are symmetric positive definite matrices; Q is chosen (usually the identity) and P is solved for.

blocks.text: Setting AᵀP + PA = −Q turns the search for V into a linear matrix equation, the Lyapunov equation. The theorem: A has all eigenvalues in the left half plane (it is Hurwitz) if and only if for every positive definite Q there is a unique positive definite P solving the equation. For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]] and Q = I, the solution is P = [[1.25, 0.25], [0.25, 0.25]], which is positive definite, so the system is stable. The level curves of xᵀPx are nested ellipses.

The Krasovskii method avoids guessing. Take V(x) = f(x)ᵀf(x) and form the Jacobian J(x) = ∂f/∂x. If Jᵀ + J is negative definite everywhere, the origin is asymptotically stable; if in addition V(x) → ∞ as ||x|| → ∞, the origin is globally asymptotically stable, provided the origin is the only equilibrium. It works directly on f with a fixed formula.

figure.caption: The test is a chain, not an equation: the system fixes f, you choose V, and the sign of V̇ decides the conclusion. Only the negative-definite branch gives asymptotic stability.

spec.title: Lyapunov test
spec.aria: A flowchart tests a positive Lyapunov function: negative derivative gives asymptotic stability, non-positive gives stability.

examples.question: The system ẋ₁ = −x₁ + x₂, ẋ₂ = −x₁ − x₂ − x₂³ has an equilibrium at the origin. Using V(x) = ½(x₁² + x₂²), show that the origin is globally asymptotically stable. Evaluate V and V̇ at x₁ = 1, x₂ = 2, with time in seconds.
steps: Equilibrium check: f(0,0) = (0, 0), so the origin is an equilibrium.
Positivity: V(0,0) = 0, and V = ½(x₁² + x₂²) > 0 whenever x ≠ 0.
Substitute: V̇ = x₁(−x₁ + x₂) + x₂(−x₁ − x₂ − x₂³).
Expand: V̇ = −x₁² + x₁x₂ − x₁x₂ − x₂² − x₂⁴; the cross terms cancel.
Result: V̇ = −x₁² − x₂² − x₂⁴ = −(x₁² + x₂² + x₂⁴) < 0 for every x ≠ 0.
So V̇ is negative definite and V is radially unbounded: globally asymptotically stable.
At the same point: V̇ = −(1 + 4 + 16) = −21 per second.
examples.answer: V̇ = −x₁² − x₂² − x₂⁴ is negative definite and V → ∞ radially, so the origin is globally asymptotically stable; at (1, 2) V = 2.5 and V̇ = −21 per second.
examples.check:
x1, x2 = 1.0, 2.0
V = 0.5*(x1**2 + x2**2)
x1dot = -x1 + x2
x2dot = -x1 - x2 - x2**3
Vdot = x1*x1dot + x2*x2dot
formula = -x1**2 - x2**2 - x2**4
assert abs(Vdot - formula) < 1e-12
print(V)
print(Vdot)

traps: V̇ ≤ 0 proves stability only. When V̇ merely vanishes on a line and the examiner asks about asymptotic stability, the safe answer is that this V does not prove asymptotic stability; the system may still be asymptotically stable, and an extra argument such as LaSalle's invariance principle is what turns the answer into yes.
V must be positive definite. A negative or sign-indefinite V is not a Lyapunov function, and multiplying a correct V by −1 destroys the test.
Sign slips in V̇: the partial ∂V/∂x₁ multiplies ẋ₁, not x₁. Cross terms like x₁x₂ usually cancel — if they do not, check the algebra before the conclusion.
A global claim needs radial unboundedness. V = x₁²/(1 + x₁²) + x₂² is positive definite but bounded along x₁, so it gives no global result.
Do not confuse Jacobian linearisation, which is local, with Lyapunov's direct method, which can be global. Failure to find a V proves nothing — the method is sufficient, not necessary.

quiz.q: Define an equilibrium point and state the three conditions on V for global asymptotic stability.
quiz.a: An equilibrium point x_e satisfies f(x_e) = 0. Conditions: V(0) = 0 and V(x) > 0 for x ≠ 0; V̇(x) < 0 for x ≠ 0; V(x) → ∞ as ||x|| → ∞.

quiz.q: Why does the direct method not need the solution x(t)?
quiz.a: V̇ = ∇V·f(x) is computed from V and the vector field f alone. The chain rule already accounts for the motion, so the sign of V̇ along all trajectories is known without integrating the state equation.

quiz.q: For ẋ = −x³ with V = ½x², compute V̇ and conclude.
quiz.a: V̇ = x·(−x³) = −x⁴, which is negative for every x ≠ 0, and V → ∞ as |x| → ∞. The origin is globally asymptotically stable.

quiz.q: A student finds V = x₁² + x₂² with V̇ = −x₂². What can be concluded, and what cannot?
quiz.a: V̇ ≤ 0, so the origin is stable. V̇ vanishes on the whole x₁ axis, so negative definiteness fails and asymptotic stability is not proved by this test alone; LaSalle's invariance principle would be needed to go further.

quiz.q: For ẋ = Ax with A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]] and Q = I, verify that P = [[1.25, 0.25], [0.25, 0.25]] solves AᵀP + PA = −Q and comment on stability.
quiz.a: Multiplying out gives AᵀP + PA = [[−1, 0], [0, −1]] = −I. P is symmetric, 1.25 > 0 and det P = 1.25(0.25) − 0.0625 = 0.25 > 0, so P is positive definite; hence A is Hurwitz and the origin is asymptotically stable.

quiz.q: State the Krasovskii method and say when it is preferred.
quiz.a: Take V(x) = f(x)ᵀf(x) and J(x) = ∂f/∂x. If Jᵀ + J is negative definite everywhere, the origin is asymptotically stable; if in addition V(x) → ∞ as ||x|| → ∞, the origin is globally asymptotically stable, provided the origin is the only equilibrium. It is preferred when no obvious energy expression exists, because it needs no guess.

quiz.q: Two candidates are offered for a system: V₁ with V̇₁ = −x₁² and V₂ with V̇₂ = −x₁² − x₂⁴. Which gives the stronger conclusion?
quiz.a: V₂. Its derivative is negative definite, so it gives asymptotic stability, while V̇₁ ≤ 0 only gives stability because it vanishes on the x₂ axis.

beyond: Not for the exam. Sum-of-squares programming asks a convex optimiser to find a polynomial V with negative derivative, certifying whole families of nonlinear plants. Control barrier functions reuse the idea for safety, keeping a drone inside a permitted set. Lyapunov arguments also supply the terminal cost and feasibility proof in nonlinear model predictive control. Search for sum-of-squares Lyapunov certificates, control barrier functions, and Lyapunov-based model predictive control.
